claims.text: High-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by selective oxidation of Ti and Cr.
Oxidizing exposure rapidly produces a duplex scale with a porous Ti-rich inner oxide and a thin Cr-rich outer layer.
Reducing exposure produces sub-stoichiometric or discontinuous oxide scales.
Sub-stoichiometric or discontinuous scales generate internal stresses and grain-boundary microcracking.
The as-fabricated alloy has a homogeneous, single-phase FCC microstructure.
The as-fabricated alloy exhibits high strength and fatigue performance.
Ti oxidizes rapidly and forms a porous inner oxide that does not provide comprehensive protection.
Cr oxidizes more slowly than Ti and forms a thinner outer layer that cannot compensate for the porous Ti-rich oxide.
Incomplete oxide formation in reducing atmospheres causes greater internal stress and microstructural degradation.
Oxidizing conditions produce a moderately protective oxide scale that thickens with exposure time and causes gradual degradation.
Reducing conditions cause more grain-boundary microcracking and void formation than the starting-state baseline.
Reducing conditions accelerate degradation relative to the starting-state baseline.
The proposed mechanism is applicable from 800 to 1200 °C for exposures of up to 1000 hours in air, O2-rich gases, or H2-containing gases.
Different degradation mechanisms may dominate outside the stated temperature, duration, and atmosphere boundaries.
Analogous complex-alloy studies support roles for Ti and Cr in oxidation or passivation behavior.
Comparing identically processed specimens under oxidizing and reducing atmospheres can distinguish the proposed gas-dependent degradation pathways.
The hypothesis is falsified if the two atmospheres produce no duplex-scale or microcracking differences and mechanical properties degrade at similar rates.
